timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What's the difference between routing and switching?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Switching connects devices on the same network. Routing connects different networks together — like local roads vs highways.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: And BGP is what handles the highways?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. BGP tells the internet how to get packets from one autonomous system to another. It's the GPS of the internet.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Easily. BGP hijacking lets an attacker announce false routes, redirecting traffic through their network before forwarding it.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: And nobody checks if the routes are real?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Mostly no. BGP was built on trust. RPKI and ROA help, but adoption is slow. Many networks still accept any route.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What about OSPF? That's for internal networks?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: OSPF shares routing tables within an autonomous system. If an attacker injects false OSPF routes, internal traffic goes haywire.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What about STP? I've heard that's vulnerable too.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: STP prevents loops in switched networks. An attacker can send fake STP packets to become the root bridge and intercept all traffic.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So both routing and switching have serious vulnerabilities?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Yes. Routing attacks can redirect the entire internet. Switching attacks can take down an entire office network.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: RPKI for BGP, BPDU guard for STP, and route filtering. But they require active configuration and maintenance.
